content: Muscle tissue, derived from the mesodermal layer of embryonic germ cells, is a specialized contractile tissue responsible for generating force and facilitating movement. Muscle cells contain contractile filaments, primarily actin and myosin, which slide past one another to produce changes in cell size and generate motion. Muscles are categorized into three types: skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle. Each type serves distinct functions, ranging from voluntary movements to involuntary processes essential for survival, such as heart contractions and peristalsis in the digestive system. Skeletal muscle, also known as voluntary muscle, is attached to bones via tendons and is responsible for locomotion and posture. While postural control is often reflexive, skeletal muscles can also be consciously controlled. In adult males, skeletal muscle constitutes approximately 40–50% of body mass, while in females, it accounts for 30–40%. Smooth muscle, in contrast, is involuntary and found in the walls of internal organs and structures, such as the gastrointestinal tract, blood vessels, and bladder. Cardiac muscle, also involuntary, is unique to the heart and shares structural similarities with skeletal muscle, including the presence of sarcomeres, but differs in its branching fiber arrangement and intercalated discs. Skeletal muscle fibers are further classified into slow-twitch (Type I) and fast-twitch (Type II) fibers. Type I fibers are rich in mitochondria, myoglobin, and capillaries, enabling sustained aerobic activity with low force output. Type II fibers, which include subtypes IIa, IIx, and IIb, are adapted for rapid, powerful contractions. Type IIa fibers are aerobic and appear red due to their high mitochondrial and capillary density. Type IIx fibers, the fastest in humans, rely on anaerobic metabolism and are less dense in mitochondria and myoglobin. Type IIb fibers, predominantly found in small animals, are glycolytic and appear white due to their low mitochondrial content. The gross anatomy of a muscle determines its functional role. The origin and insertion points, as well as the muscle's cross-sectional area, influence the force it can generate. Pennate muscles, which have fibers oriented at an angle to the line of action, allow for greater force production in a compact size but exhibit reduced length changes. Examples include the rectus femoris. In contrast, non-pennate muscles have fibers aligned parallel to the line of action, optimizing speed and range of motion. At the microscopic level, muscle tissue is composed of muscle fibers, which are organized into bundles called fascicles. Each muscle fiber contains myofibrils, which are further divided into sarcomeres, the basic contractile units composed of actin and myosin filaments. Surrounding each muscle fiber is the endomysium, while the perimysium encases fascicles, and the epimysium envelops the entire muscle. Muscle spindles, embedded within muscles, provide sensory feedback to the central nervous system, aiding in proprioception and motor control. Muscle contraction is driven by the interaction of actin and myosin filaments, powered by adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Skeletal muscle contraction is initiated by electrical impulses from motor neurons, while cardiac and smooth muscle contractions are regulated by pacemaker cells. Muscles store energy in the form of creatine phosphate and glycogen, which can be metabolized anaerobically or aerobically depending on the activity's intensity and duration. Cardiac muscle, uniquely, can metabolize all three macronutrients (carbohydrates, fats, and proteins) efficiently without a warm-up period. The nervous system plays a critical role in muscle control. The efferent pathways transmit motor commands from the brain to muscles, while afferent pathways relay sensory information back to the central nervous system. Reflexive movements bypass the brain, relying on spinal cord circuits, whereas voluntary movements involve complex interactions between the motor cortex, basal ganglia, cerebellum, and pyramidal tracts. Exercise influences muscle physiology and fiber utilization. Aerobic exercise predominantly engages Type I fibers, relying on oxygen and fat metabolism for sustained activity. Anaerobic exercise, such as sprinting or weightlifting, recruits Type II fibers and relies on ATP and glucose for short bursts of high-intensity activity. Training adaptations include increased capillary density, mitochondrial content, and the ability to clear lactic acid, which can be metabolized by other tissues or converted back to pyruvate in the liver. Muscle diseases, such as myopathies and neuromuscular disorders, can manifest as weakness, spasticity, or myalgia. Diagnostic tools include creatine kinase assays, electromyography, and muscle biopsies. Conditions like sarcopenia, a gradual loss of muscle mass with aging, result from reduced satellite cell function and decreased growth factor sensitivity. Muscle atrophy can also occur in cachexia, heart failure, or liver disease. Muscle strength is influenced by physiological, neurological, and mechanical factors. While the number of muscle fibers remains constant, hypertrophy increases their size. Notable muscles include the masseter, which exerts the greatest force relative to its size, and the heart, which performs continuous work throughout a lifetime. The efficiency of muscle contraction, defined as the ratio of mechanical work to metabolic energy expenditure, ranges from 14% to 27%. Bodybuilding focuses on maximizing muscle hypertrophy through resistance training, adequate nutrition, and rest. Evolutionarily, skeletal and cardiac muscles predate the vertebrate-arthropod divergence, indicating their development in a common ancestor over 700 million years ago.
